questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which is the first bone to ossify in the human body?
questions.explanation: The clavicle is the first bone to ossify in the human body. It begins ossification in the 5th-6th weeks of intrauterine life. The clavicle is a blend of condensed mesenchyme in the early embryonic phase. At its terminal ends, early cartilage transformation (pre-cartilage) takes place; intramembranous centres of ossification appear and fuse in the mesenchyme between them. Hence, the clavicle ossifies partly in membrane and partly in cartilage.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following is false about clavicle?

options.text: Ossify partly in membrane and partly in cartilage
Transmits part of the weight of upper limb to the axial skeleton
It is subcutaneous throughout its length
Fractures typically occur at the junction of medial 1/3rd and lateral 2/3rd

questions.correctAnswerText: Fractures typically occur at the junction of medial 1/3rd and lateral 2/3rd
questions.explanation: Fractures of the clavicle typically occur at the junction of the medial 3/5th and lateral 2/5th. The middle-third or midshaft region is the commonest fracture site, especially at this junction. It is the junction where the two primary ossification centres meet and also the transition from a more curved medial segment to a flatter lateral segment, making it a high-risk site. The proximal fragment is displaced upward by sternocleidomastoid and the distal fragment downward by pectoralis major and gravity.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which ligament transmits the weight of the upper limb to the axial skeleton?
questions.explanation: The weight of the upper limb is transmitted to the axial skeleton by the coracoclavicular and costoclavicular ligaments. The source describes the pathway as: upper limb → coracoclavicular ligament → clavicle → costoclavicular ligament → axial skeleton (sternum and 1st rib). It notes that the costoclavicular ligament transmits weight to the axial skeleton via the clavicle; the coracoclavicular ligament transmits weight of the upper limb to the clavicle; and the sternoclavicular ligament transmits weight to the axial skeleton via the clavicle inferomedially.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: In a patient with a coracoid fracture, the action of which of the following muscle is not hindered?
questions.explanation: In a patient with a coracoid fracture, the action of the long head of triceps muscle is not hindered. The long head of triceps attaches to the infraglenoid tubercle on the lateral border of the scapula, not to the coracoid process. Coracoid process attachments include the origins of coracobrachialis and short head of biceps, insertion of pectoralis minor, and the coracoacromial, coracoclavicular and coracohumeral ligaments.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A 16-year-old athlete was diagnosed with an isolated avulsion fracture of the lesser tubercle of the humerus. The forceful contraction of which of the following muscles causes this fracture?
questions.explanation: Forceful contraction of the subscapularis can cause an isolated avulsion fracture of the lesser tubercle of the humerus because subscapularis inserts on the lesser tubercle. Forceful contraction while resisting abduction and external rotation can avulse this insertion. The other rotator-cuff insertions shown are supraspinatus, infraspinatus and teres minor on the greater tubercle.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which muscle is attached to the floor of the structure marked A?
questions.explanation: The structure marked A is the intertubercular sulcus (bicipital groove), and latissimus dorsi is attached to its floor. The intertubercular sulcus lies between the greater and lesser tubercles. Attachments around it are: lateral lip - pectoralis major; medial lip - teres major; floor - latissimus dorsi. Contents include the long head of biceps and the ascending branch of the anterior circumflex humeral artery. The source memory tip is 'Lady between two majors': latissimus dorsi lies between pectoralis major laterally and teres major medially.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A 25-year-old man comes with sudden pain in his right shoulder. He complains that he is not able to move his right arm. After evaluation, a diagnosis of shoulder dislocation was made. Which of the following statements is false regarding this joint?

options.text: The glenohumeral joint is the most frequently dislocated joint in the body
As mobility of the joint increases, stability also increases
The shoulder joint dislocation is rare in children
Anterior dislocation is more common than a posterior dislocation

questions.correctAnswerText: As mobility of the joint increases, stability also increases
questions.explanation: As mobility increases, stability is lost in a joint. The glenohumeral joint is the most mobile joint in the body and is very unstable. It is the most frequently dislocated joint. Shoulder dislocation is more common in adults and is rare in children. Anterior dislocation is much more common than posterior dislocation.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A 17-year-old boy presented with instability of the shoulder joint following sports trauma. Injury to all of the following structures may cause this condition except:

options.text: Tendon of long head of biceps

questions.explanation: Teres major has no role in maintaining stability of the shoulder joint. Because the humeral head is larger than the glenoid cavity, the shoulder is predisposed to displacement. Stability is provided by the rotator cuff (supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor and subscapularis), the tendon of the long head of biceps, and the coracoacromial ligament. Degeneration or tear of these structures leads to instability. The shoulder joint is least protected inferiorly; the capsule is loose and only the long head of triceps crosses the joint inferiorly.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: In a patient with shoulder dislocation, which of the following muscle action is not hindered?
questions.explanation: Pectoralis minor has no action at the shoulder joint. It originates from the 3rd-5th ribs near their costochondral junctions and inserts on the medial border and upper surface of the coracoid process. It is an accessory muscle of inspiration and stabilizes the scapula by pulling it anteriorly and inferiorly. The source provides a movement table for the shoulder joint.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which movement range is increased at the glenohumeral joint due to the lateral rotation of the humerus?
questions.explanation: Lateral rotation of the humerus increases the range of abduction. During abduction without rotation, the greater tubercle comes in contact with the coracoacromial arch and prevents further abduction. With lateral rotation toward 180 degrees, the tubercles rotate posteriorly and the more articular surface continues to elevate, increasing the range of abduction.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A normal scapulohumeral rhythm is in the ratio of:
questions.explanation: A normal scapulohumeral rhythm is 2:1. Scapulohumeral rhythm is the ratio of glenohumeral movement to scapulothoracic movement during arm elevation. For example, during 90 degrees of abduction, glenohumeral elevation is about 60 degrees and scapulothoracic rotation about 30 degrees.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following structure is intracapsular?
questions.explanation: The long head of biceps is intracapsular. The fibrous capsule of the shoulder attaches medially to the glenoid neck at a variable distance from the glenoid labrum. The capsule includes the supraglenoid tubercle, to which the long head of biceps attaches, so the long-head tendon lies within the capsule.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following muscles form the border of rotator interval?
questions.explanation: The rotator interval is the area between supraspinatus and subscapularis. It is a medially based triangular area not covered by capsule. It lies between the superior edge of subscapularis and the anterior edge of supraspinatus, with the coracoid as the medial boundary of the interval. It is reinforced by the coracohumeral ligament, superior glenohumeral ligament, and fibres from the supraspinatus tendon laterally.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following structures of the scapula is palpable in the infraclavicular fossa?
questions.explanation: The part of the scapula marked A is palpable in the infraclavicular fossa and is the coracoid process. The apex of the coracoid process lies approximately 2.5 cm below the clavicle, immediately lateral to the infraclavicular fossa (deltopectoral triangle), and can be palpated below the clavicle.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Movements of pronation and supination occurs in all of the following joints except:
questions.explanation: Pronation and supination do not occur at the radiocarpal (wrist) joint. These movements mainly occur at the humeroradial, superior radioulnar and inferior radioulnar joints. The middle radioulnar joint is a fibrous syndesmosis that binds radius and ulna and helps transmit weight from radius toward ulna.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: During an intracapsular arthroscopy, which of the following structure cannot be seen?
questions.explanation: During intracapsular arthroscopy the lateral epicondyle cannot be seen because it is extracapsular. The elbow joint capsule is attached anteriorly just above the coronoid and radial fossae and posteriorly above the olecranon fossa. The source also notes that the medial epicondyle is extracapsular.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: What is the normal approximate carrying angle?
questions.explanation: The average carrying angle is approximately 17 degrees. It is the angle between the fully supinated forearm and the long axis of the humerus when the elbow is fully extended. It is usually about 10-15 degrees in males and more than 15 degrees in females, varies among individuals, and increases with age. Clinically, the contralateral side should be compared. The source notes that about 5-15 degrees is considered normal clinically; the carrying angle decreases in cubitus varus and increases in cubitus valgus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: The middle radioulnar joint is an example of a:
questions.explanation: The middle radioulnar joint is a fibrous joint (syndesmosis). Radius and ulna are united by the proximal radioulnar joint, middle radioulnar joint, and distal radioulnar joint. Proximal and distal radioulnar joints are uniaxial pivot synovial joints involved in pronation and supination. The middle radioulnar joint is formed by the oblique cord and interosseous membrane as syndesmoses. The source also summarizes structural joint classes: fibrous (sutures, syndesmosis, gomphosis), cartilaginous (primary/synchondrosis and secondary/symphysis), and synovial (ball-and-socket, saddle, condylar/bicondylar, ellipsoid, hinge, pivot/trochoid and plane).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A golfer hurt himself after he accidentally hit the ground while taking a shot. He has tenderness in the area shown in the image below. On examination, he has pain radiating to his ring and little finger. Which of the following bones is most likely to be fractured?
questions.explanation: Tenderness in the shown hypothenar region with pain radiating to the ring and little finger is suggestive of a hook of hamate fracture. The pain distribution is related to the close proximity of the ulnar nerve, particularly its deep branch. The hamate is a cuneiform carpal bone with a hamulus (hook) projecting from the distal part of its rough palmar surface. The source also gives the carpal-bone mnemonic: She (Scaphoid) Looks (Lunate) Too (Triquetral) Pretty (Pisiform) - Try (Trapezium) To (Trapezoid) Catch (Capitate) Her (Hamate).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A child falls from his bicycle and injures his hand. On X-ray, a fracture of the first metacarpal bone is noticed. Where is the epiphysis of the affected bone?
questions.explanation: The epiphysis of the first metacarpal is at the base; all other metacarpals have their epiphysis at the head. The first metacarpal is the shortest and stoutest metacarpal. Its base has a convexoconcave articular surface for a saddle synovial joint with trapezium. The first metacarpal fracture at the base is called Bennett's fracture. The source radiograph also illustrates early ossification at about 2.5 years.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: All of the following take part in the formation of the wrist joint, except:
questions.explanation: The distal end of the ulna does not take part in formation of the radiocarpal (wrist) joint. The wrist is a synovial, biaxial, ellipsoid joint formed by the distal radius, articular disc of triangular fibrocartilage, and scaphoid, lunate and triquetrum. In neutral position, only scaphoid and lunate are in contact with the radius and articular disc; triquetrum comes into apposition with the disc only in full adduction.
